title.en: Bran Og and the Giant Bird That Proved Oisin's Word
title.zh: 布蘭·奧格與印證歐辛之言的巨鳥

texts.period: Fenian-Christian interface, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Patrick calls Oisin's boast a lie — a blackbird quarter bigger than beef, a rowan berry bigger than a churn. Oisin rears the one pup that grips a raw hide, keeps it a year without blood or daylight, digs up the Fianna's horn, iron ball and sword, and blows three blasts that bring down three clouds of birds; Bran Og kills the biggest, goes mad with its blood, and dies by Oisin's iron ball — and inside the bird lie the rowan berry and the ivy leaf. "Truth that was in our hearts, and strength in our arms, and fulfilment in our tongues."
summary.zh: 帕特里克斥歐辛之言為謊——「黑鳥腿大過牛肉、花楸果大過牛油攪桶」。歐辛育成唯一咬住生皮不放的幼犬，養其一年不見血不見光；掘出菲亞納號角、鐵球與寶劍，三吹角聲引下三雲群鳥；布蘭·奧格誅最大之鳥、飲血而狂，死於歐辛鐵球之下——鳥腹中竟有花楸果與大過烤盤的常春藤葉。「心懷真理，臂有強力，言出必行。」

sensitivity.note: The tale-type is the truth-proof (aim-demonstration) between saint and pagan hero; the pre-Christian world's enormity vouched by physical relics is the cycle's central comparative device. The madness-and-death of Bran Og repeats the hound-death pattern of the corpus. Pin at Gleann-na-Smol, named in the tale.

passages.text: There was great anger on Oisin, and he went where there was a litter of pups, and he bade a serving-boy to nail up the hide of a freshly killed bullock to the wall, and to throw the pups against it one by one; and every one that he threw fell down from the hide till it came to the last, and he held on to it with his teeth and his nails. "Rear that one, and drown all the rest." Then he bade the boy to keep the pup in a dark place, and to care it well, and never to let it taste blood or see the daylight; and at the end of a year Oisin gave it the name of Bran Og, young Bran.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And one day he called to the serving-boy to come on a journey with him, and to bring the pup in a chain; and they passed by Slieve-nam-ban, where the witches of the Sidhe do be spinning with their spinning-wheels, and then turned eastward into Gleann-na-Smol. And Oisin raised a rock that was there, and he bade the lad take from under it three things, a great sounding horn of the Fianna, and a ball of iron they had for throwing, and a very sharp sword. "My thousand farewells to the day when you were put here!"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Oisin took the horn himself, and blew three great blasts on it, and the boy saw three great clouds coming and settling down in the valley: the first cloud a flight of very big birds, and the second a flight of birds bigger again, and the third flight of the biggest and the blackest birds the world ever saw. "What is the dog doing?" "The eyes are starting from his head, and there is not a rib of hair on him but is standing up." "Let him loose now." Bran Og rushed down and made an attack on one of the birds, the biggest of all, that had a shadow like a cloud, and at last made an end of it, and lapped its blood; but madness came on him, and he came rushing back towards Oisin, his jaws open and his eyes like fire, and Oisin made a cast of the iron ball that went into the mouth and the throat of the dog, and choked him, and he fell down the slope, twisting and foaming.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And Oisin bade the lad cut open the body of the bird, and in it he found a rowan berry, the biggest he had ever seen, and an ivy leaf that was bigger than the biggest griddle. So Oisin went to where S. Patrick was, and showed him the quarter of the bird that was bigger than any quarter of a bullock, and the rowan berry that was bigger than a churning of butter, and the leaf: "And you know now, Patrick of the Bells, that I told no lie; and it is what kept us all through our lifetime, truth that was in our hearts, and strength in our arms, and fulfilment in our tongues."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Arguments of Oisin and Patrick

region.en: House of S. Patrick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭聖帕特里克居所（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian-Christian dialogue poems (Acallam-derived), medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: The poets of Ireland put down afterwards the two voices of the great quarrel: Patrick, that the Fianna are condemned to hell for their unbelief, and Oisin, that Finn the open-handed could not be held in any house made by God or devils — "if Osgar my own son is there, there is not in hell or in the Heaven of God a troop so great that he could not destroy it." Between the rounds run the catalogues of Finn's music and the hounds of the first hunt, and Oisin's word at the last: "I will cry my fill, but not for God, but because Finn and the Fianna are not living."
summary.zh: 愛爾蘭詩人後世記下了這場大爭論的兩種聲音：帕特里克稱菲亞納因不信而入地獄；歐辛則言——「慷慨的芬恩絕不會被神或魔所造的任何屋宇困住；若吾子奧斯加在彼處，地獄與天國中再無一支軍隊能抵擋他的毀滅」。爭論間穿插芬恩樂音的清單與初獵之犬的名冊；歐辛臨終之言：「我要哭盡我的淚——不是為了神，而是因為芬恩與菲亞納已不在人間。」

sensitivity.note: This is the pagan-Christian dialogue literature (Agallamh tradition) — a contested religious boundary treated here as documentary comparative material; the claim that the Fianna are in hell is Patrick's in-story position, not the corpus's. The catalogue of Finn's music recurs as the cycle's aesthetic witness. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: S. Patrick took in hand to convert Oisin, and to bring him to baptism, but it was no easy work he had to do, and everything he would say, Oisin would have an answer for it. PATRICK: "Oisin, it is long your sleep is. Rise up and listen to the Psalm." OISIN: "My readiness and my strength are gone from me since Finn has no armies living; I have no liking for clerks, their music is not sweet to me after his. I have heard music was sweeter than your music: the song of the blackbird in Leiter Laoi, and the sound of the Dord Fiann; the cry of the hounds was better to me than the noise of your schools, Patrick. Little Nut, little Nut of my heart, the little dwarf that was with Finn, when he would make tunes and songs he would put us all into deep sleep."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: PATRICK: "All the gold you and Finn used to be giving out, it is little it does for you now; he is in Hell in bonds because he did treachery and oppression." OISIN: "It is little I believe of your truth, man from Rome with the white books, Finn the open-handed head of the Fianna to be in the hands of devils or demons. If the sons of Morna were within it, or the strong men of the sons of Baiscne, they would take Finn out of it, or they would have the house for themselves." PATRICK: "If the five provinces of Ireland were within it, or the strong seven battalions of the Fianna, they could not bring Finn out of it." OISIN: "If Faolan and Goll were living, and brown-haired Diarmuid and brave Osgar, Finn of the Fianna could not be held in any house that was made by God or devils... If there was a place above or below better than the Heaven of God, it is there Finn would go, and all that are with him of his people."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: OISIN: "O Patrick, where was your God when the two came over the sea that brought away the queen of Lochlann of the Ships? Where was He when Dearg came, the son of the King of Lochlann of the golden shields? Why did not the King of Heaven protect them from the blows of the big man? Or when Tailc, son of Treon, came, the man that did great slaughter on the Fianna; it was not by God that champion fell, but by Osgar, in the sight of all. Many a battle and many a victory was gained by the Fianna of Ireland; I never heard any great deed was done by the King of Saints, or that He ever reddened His hand." And at the last Oisin said: "My story is sorrowful. The sound of your voice is not pleasant to me. I will cry my fill, but not for God, but because Finn and the Fianna are not living."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Oisin's Laments for the Household of Finn

region.en: House of S. Patrick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭聖帕特里克居所（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian-Christian interface, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book XI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Blind among Patrick's household, Oisin makes the laments that are remembered yet — "I saw the household of Finn; it was not the household of a soft race" — and, one night when the servants would not go out with him on his shoulders to mind the cattle, they lie to him of storms; a serving-girl truer than the rest sends him out, and the boy on his back dashes water in his face with a birch broom until Oisin finds the night quiet and asks no more news of the weather from the servants.
summary.zh: 失明的歐辛居於帕特里克家中，詠出流傳至今的哀歌——「我見過芬恩的家室；那絕非柔弱之族的家室」。一夜僕人拒絕讓他如常背負自己去看牛群，便謊報風雨；一名侍女較其餘人誠實，請他起身外出；背上的僕人以樺皮帚撩水入他面上冒充雨滴——直到歐辛發覺夜空無恙，此後再不向僕人打聽天氣。

sensitivity.note: The lying-weather-servants episode is a set-piece of the Oisin-in-Patrick's-house cycle (the blind hero cheated by Christian household — the corpus's comment on the new order); the laments are verse-transmitted memoria. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: And Oisin used to be making laments, and sometimes he would be making praises of the old times and of Finn: "I saw the household of Finn; it was not the household of a soft race; I had a vision of that man yesterday. I saw the household of the High King, he with the brown, sweet-voiced son; I never saw a better man. I saw the household of Finn; no one saw it as I saw it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And when Oisin had no sight left at all, he used every night to put up one of the serving-men on his shoulders, and to bring him out to see how were the cattle doing. And one night the servants had no mind to go, and they agreed together to tell him it was a very bad night. And it is what the first of them said: "It is outside there is a heavy sound with the heavy water dropping from the tops of trees; the sound of the waves is not to be heard for the loud splashing of the rain." And then the next one said: "The trees of the wood are shivering, and the birch is turning black; the snow is killing the birds; that is the story outside." And the third said: "It is to the east they have turned their face, the white snow and the dark rain."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: But there was a serving-girl in the house, and she said: "Rise up, Oisin, and go out to the white-headed cows, since the cold wind is plucking the trees from the hills." Oisin went out then, and the serving-man on his shoulders; but it is what the serving-man did, he brought a vessel of water and a birch broom with him, and he was dashing water in Oisin's face, the way he would think it was rain. But when they came to the pen where the cattle were, Oisin found the night was quiet, and after that he asked no more news of the weather from the servants.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book XI, ch. IV; not verbatim.
